characters: Abigail: a 14-year-old girl in glasses and a lab coat, leader of the group.
Jerome: a 14-year-old boy who is clever but always busy with his phone.
Sandra and Sampson: two group members, 13 and 14, sticking card and testing water.
Madam Tetteh-Quao: the science teacher, in a green cardigan, with a clipboard of marking sheets.

narrationPlan.voice: Lively students; a calm, fair voice for Madam Tetteh-Quao
narrationPlan.pace: Brisk and funny, steady at the polite conversation (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Quirky, bubbly science-lab music; a calm resolution tune near the end (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The school, students and teacher are invented. The model filter is a classroom demonstration and does not make water safe to drink.
The letter on page 7 is exam-safe: full words, correct spelling and a closing question that invites a reply.
The story shows a group problem solved by conversation rather than blame. Teachers can discuss when it is also right to involve an adult.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that the model filter is described as a demonstration only and that no one is encouraged to drink filtered water.
Check the pen-pal letter ending (“Yours ever”) and the address-and-date line against the NaCCA informal-letter lesson and the marking scheme.
Check that the story does not shame the shy student and shows a fair way to handle group conflict.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about group work, fairness and honest speech in a science fair. It also models a pen-pal letter in exam-safe English.
learningGoals: Describe a kind way to speak to a teammate who is not helping.
Rewrite chat-style words in full, correct English.

subjectLinks.subject: Information and Communication Technology
subjectLinks.link: Responsible use of phones and posting

beforeReading: Ask: have you ever worked in a group where one person did not help? What did you do?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners to suggest other kind ways to start that conversation.
afterReading: Write a pen-pal letter describing a group project.
Make a task chart for a real class project.
discussion: When should a teammate talk to a friend, and when should they talk to the teacher?
Why is credit for others’ work important?
reflection: What job in a group suits you best, and why?

mathsExtension.task: The group scored 18 marks for the model and 22 for the poster and presentation. The total is out of 50. What fraction is lost?
mathsExtension.answer: 18 + 22 = 40, so 10 out of 50 or one fifth is lost.

mathsExtension.task: The group worked 3 hours a day for 4 days. How many hours?

support: Provide a letter frame with sentence starters and a list of exam-safe linking words: first, then, however, finally.
stretch: Build the filter at school with an adult, test with muddy water and write a short lab report. Do not drink the water.

culturalNotes: The school, students and teacher are invented. The model filter is a classroom demonstration and does not make water safe to drink.
The letter on page 7 is exam-safe: full words, correct spelling and a closing question that invites a reply.
The story shows a group problem solved by conversation rather than blame. Teachers can discuss when it is also right to involve an adult.
localiseThis: Use real science fair formats in your school and local water examples.
Never let learners drink water from a model.

factCheck.claim: Text abbreviations such as “u” for “you”, “ur” for “your” and “tnx” for “thanks” are examples of the social media language WAEC has warned students not to use in exam scripts.
factCheck.explanation: From WAEC’s statement in September 2026 and earlier reports of examiners’ concerns.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Social media language creeping into students’ examination scripts: WAEC” (7 September 2026); Junior Graphic, “Youngsters’ abbreviated words and exam results” (2015).
